title: How do String and StringBuffer handle memory differently (immutable new objects vs mutable char array)?
shortTitle: How do String and StringBuffer handle memory differently?

s1_definition.profdef: `String` handles memory as immutable objects: each String wraps a fixed character array, and any modifying operation allocates a brand-new String with a new array, leaving the original for the garbage collector, so repeated edits create many short-lived objects. `StringBuffer` handles memory as a single mutable, growable character array held inside one object: modifications like append write into that same array in place, and the array only grows, typically doubling, when capacity is exceeded, so building a large string reuses one backing array instead of allocating a new object per edit. Consequently, String is memory-efficient for fixed values but wasteful for repeated edits, while StringBuffer is memory-efficient for building and mutating strings.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, editing a String is like a clerk who, to add one line to a statement, photocopies the entire statement onto a fresh page, writes the new line, and throws the old page in the bin; after a hundred edits the bin is overflowing with discarded pages. A StringBuffer is like a clerk who writes on one long scroll, simply adding each new line at the bottom, and only occasionally tapes on a longer blank extension when the scroll runs out of room. The scroll approach reuses the same paper and barely creates any waste, which is why it is the right tool when the record is built up piece by piece.
s1_definition.oneliner: String allocates a new immutable object per edit creating garbage, while StringBuffer mutates one growable backing array in place and only resizes when full.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `String` handles memory as immutable objects: each String wraps a fixed character array, and any modifying operation allocates a brand-new String with a new array, leaving the original for the garbage collector, so repeated edits create many short-lived objects. `StringBuffer` handles memory as a single mutable, growable character array held inside one object: modifications like append write into that same array in place, and the array only grows, typically doubling, when capacity is exceeded, so building a large string reuses one backing array instead of allocating a new object per edit. Consequently, String is memory-efficient for fixed values but wasteful for repeated edits, while StringBuffer is memory-efficient for building and mutating strings.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, editing a String is like a clerk who, to add one line to a statement, photocopies the entire statement onto a fresh page, writes the new line, and throws the old page in the bin; after a hundred edits the bin is overflowing with discarded pages. A StringBuffer is like a clerk who writes on one long scroll, simply adding each new line at the bottom, and only occasionally tapes on a longer blank extension when the scroll runs out of room. The scroll approach reuses the same paper and barely creates any waste, which is why it is the right tool when the record is built up piece by piece.

**One line to remember:** String allocates a new immutable object per edit creating garbage, while StringBuffer mutates one growable backing array in place and only resizes when full.

sections.s2_technical:
A String object holds a reference to a private final character array, historically a char array and since Java 9 a byte array with a coder flag for compactness. Because the array and the reference are final, the String can never change. Every operation that appears to modify a String, such as concat, substring, replace, or plus, allocates a new array, copies the relevant characters, and wraps them in a new String object. The old String becomes eligible for garbage collection if nothing else references it. So a sequence of edits creates a chain of intermediate String objects and arrays, all short-lived. In a loop this is quadratic in both time and allocation, which is a well-known source of memory churn.

A StringBuffer object holds a mutable, growable backing array plus a count of how many characters are currently used. When you append, it writes the new characters directly into the existing array and increases the count, with no new object allocated, as long as there is spare capacity. When the array fills, the buffer allocates a larger array, typically about double the current size, copies the existing characters once, and continues. Because growth doubles capacity, the number of reallocations across many appends is logarithmic, giving amortized linear cost. So building a large string with a StringBuffer, or a StringBuilder, uses essentially one backing array that grows a handful of times, rather than thousands of discarded objects.

The memory consequence is stark for repeated edits. Concatenating in a loop with String allocates on the order of the square of the length in total characters copied and creates many garbage objects, pressuring the garbage collector and hurting throughput. The same build with a StringBuffer allocates roughly linear total memory and creates very few objects.

A senior nuance is capacity management: if you can estimate the final size, constructing the buffer with that initial capacity avoids even the doubling reallocations, which matters for large statements and reports. Another nuance is that String's immutability, while costly for edits, is exactly what enables safe sharing, pooling, and hash caching, so the right design is to use StringBuffer or StringBuilder to build the text and then produce a single immutable String with toString for sharing and storage. This build-then-freeze pattern gives both efficient construction and safe sharing, which is the standard approach in banking report and statement generation.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank generates large statements and noticed heavy garbage collection when building them by String concatenation. This is exactly String's per-edit allocation creating many short-lived objects.

Problem 2 — Rebuilding with a StringBuffer that has a pre-sized capacity cut allocations dramatically because it reuses one growable array. This is exactly StringBuffer's in-place mutation and controlled growth.

Problem 3 — The final statement is produced once as an immutable String via toString for safe storage and sharing. This is exactly the build-then-freeze pattern.

The code has a `StatementMemoryDemo` main class that builds the same statement both ways and reports the buffer's capacity growth versus the String approach's object churn, using a `StatementWriter` with both methods.
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/memory/StatementMemoryDemo.java

# Run
java -cp out com.bank.memory.StatementMemoryDemo

# Optional: observe GC activity difference
java -verbose:gc -cp out com.bank.memory.StatementMemoryDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: an account SAV2001 and 10000 statement lines, built once with String concatenation and once with a StringBuffer.

Step 1: The String approach starts with a header string. In each of 10000 iterations, the plus operator allocates a new character array, copies everything accumulated so far plus the new line, and wraps it in a new String.

Step 2: Each iteration leaves the previous String as garbage. After 10000 iterations, roughly 10001 intermediate String objects have been created and discarded, and the total characters copied grow with the square of the line count.

Step 3: This flood of short-lived objects pressures the garbage collector, which must repeatedly reclaim them, hurting throughput, which is the memory cost of immutability under repeated edits.

Step 4: The StringBuffer approach creates one buffer with a pre-sized backing array large enough for the whole statement, so no growth reallocation is even needed.

Step 5: Each of the 10000 appends writes directly into that same array and bumps the count, allocating no new object per line. The one backing array is reused throughout.

Step 6: A single toString at the end produces one immutable String for safe storage and sharing. The contrast is thousands of garbage objects for String concatenation versus essentially one reused array plus a final String for the StringBuffer, which is why StringBuffer or StringBuilder is the right memory choice for building text.

```text
WARNING: String approach created ~10001 intermediate String objects (garbage)
INFO: StringBuffer built length=68894 reusing ONE growable array
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  ─── String (immutable, per-edit allocation) ───
  "hdr" ─+→ NEW String#1 ─+→ NEW String#2 ─+→ ... ─+→ NEW String#10000
            (discard)        (discard)                 (final)
  → ~10001 objects created, O(n^2) chars copied → heavy GC

  ─── StringBuffer (one growable array) ───
  [ backing char[] capacity=120000 ]  (pre-sized)
     append → write in place, count++   (no new object)
     append → write in place, count++
     ... (grows ×2 ONLY if capacity exceeded)
  → toString() once → ONE immutable String  (build-then-freeze)
  → ~1 array reused, O(n) total → minimal GC
```

  │ Batch job  │────────→ │ StatementWriter   │───────→ │ PDF / S3     │
  │ (EOM)      │          │ StringBuffer      │         └──────────────┘

  Buffer-build keeps heap/GC flat even for huge monthly statements.

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Memory Model Comparison ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                 String                         │
  │ - private final byte[] value (fixed)           │
  │ edit → NEW byte[] + NEW String (old → garbage) │
  │ loop edit → O(n^2) copies, O(n) garbage objects│
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │                 StringBuffer                   │
  │ - byte[] value (growable)                      │
  │ - int count (used length)                      │
  │ append → write in place; grow ×2 when full     │
  │ loop append → O(n) total, ~log n reallocations │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Build-then-freeze pattern:
   1 build text with StringBuffer/StringBuilder (mutable, cheap)
   2 toString() → one immutable String (shareable, poolable, keyable)
  Pre-size: new StringBuffer(estimatedLength) → avoid even ×2 resizes.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
String and StringBuffer handle memory in fundamentally different ways because one is immutable and the other is mutable. A String wraps a fixed, final character array, so it can never change. Every operation that appears to modify a String, like concat, substring, or the plus operator, actually allocates a brand-new array, copies the characters, and wraps them in a new String object, leaving the old one as garbage. So a sequence of edits produces a chain of short-lived intermediate objects, and doing this in a loop is quadratic in both time and total characters copied, which creates a lot of garbage and pressures the collector.

A StringBuffer, by contrast, holds a single mutable, growable backing array together with a count of how many characters are used. When I append, it writes the new characters directly into that same array and bumps the count, with no new object allocated, as long as there is spare capacity. Only when the array fills does it allocate a larger array, typically about double, copy the existing characters once, and continue. Because capacity doubles, the number of reallocations over many appends is logarithmic, so building a large string is amortized linear and reuses essentially one array rather than discarding thousands of objects.

I measured this on a ten-thousand-line statement: the String concatenation approach created about ten thousand intermediate String objects and churned the heap, while the StringBuffer approach reused one pre-sized array and allocated almost nothing per line.

The senior points I always add are two. First, capacity management matters: if I can estimate the final size, I construct the buffer with that initial capacity, which avoids even the doubling reallocations, and that genuinely helps for large banking statements and reports. Second, String's immutability, though costly for editing, is exactly what makes it safe to share, pool, cache its hash, and use as a key. So the right design is the build-then-freeze pattern: I use a StringBuffer or StringBuilder to construct the text cheaply and mutably, then call toString once to produce a single immutable String for storage and sharing. That combination gives me efficient construction and safe sharing at the same time, which is precisely how we generate statements in our banking system while keeping heap usage and garbage collection flat even at large scale.

---

keyPoints: String: new object for every modification — old object becomes garbage
StringBuffer/StringBuilder: modifies internal char[] in place, resizes when needed
Initial capacity: 16 characters, doubles when exceeded
Memory-efficient for repeated modifications — avoids creating garbage
